Let’s talk about the concept of *sonder*—and the strange, quiet places where human lives intersect without ever really touching.

If you’ve never come across the word, "sonder" was coined a few years ago by writer John Koenig in *The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows*. It describes the realization that each random passerby is living a life as vivid and complex as your own—populated with their own ambitions, friends, routines, worries, and inherited craziness. 

We logically know this, of course. Nobody walks around genuinely believing they are the only real person on Earth and everyone else is just a cardboard cutout placed there for ambiance. Yet, because we are trapped behind our own eyes, we are naturally the protagonists of our own stories. The barista who hands you your coffee is just "the barista." The guy driving too slowly in the left lane is just "an obstacle." 

Until, suddenly, they aren't.

Sometimes you catch a detail that breaks the illusion. You’re sitting on a train, and you see an older woman staring at a text message, her thumb hovering over the keyboard, a look of profound conflict on her face. You see a man in a sharp suit carrying a single, slightly wilted balloon at 11:00 PM. You drive past an apartment building at dusk, and in a single lit window on the fourth floor, you see someone dancing alone in their kitchen while stirring a pot on the stove.

For a fraction of a second, the veil drops. You realize that the person in that fourth-floor window has a favorite childhood memory. They have a song that makes them cry, a secret they’ve never told anyone, a specific way they like their toast, and a fear that keeps them awake at 3:00 AM. You are just a pair of headlights passing below their window—an extra in *their* movie.

What fascinates me most are the physical spaces where these millions of invisible stories overlap. 

Think about a used bookstore. You pick up a paperback from 1984. Someone folded the corner of page 112. Why did they stop there? Did their train arrive? Did the phone ring with news that changed their life, and they never picked the book up again? Sometimes there’s an inscription on the inside cover: *To Sarah, May you always find what you’re looking for. Love, Dad, Christmas '98.* How did that book get from a living room in 1998 to a dusty shelf in a thrift store twenty-six years later? 

Or think about airports at 5:00 AM. It is a liminal space, out of time. You have people in sweatpants drinking overpriced beer because, to their internal clock, it's 8:00 PM. You have someone flying toward the best week of their life—a wedding, a long-awaited vacation, a reunion—sitting right next to someone flying toward the worst week of theirs—a funeral, a goodbye. Everyone is sitting in the same uncomfortable vinyl chairs, breathing the same recycled air, completely oblivious to the emotional gravity of the person three feet away.

There is something deeply comforting about this. When our own problems feel monumental, when our anxieties feel all-consuming, it helps to zoom out. It helps to look at a sprawling city from an airplane window at night, seeing that vast web of golden streetlamps, and realizing that beneath that glow are millions of epics unfolding simultaneously. Heartbreaks, triumphs, mundane Tuesday nights, first kisses, last breaths, burnt dinners, and inside jokes. 

It makes you feel very small, yes. But it also makes you part of something incomprehensibly vast. You are a thread in a massive, chaotic, beautiful tapestry, brushing up against a thousand other threads every single day.
